\title{When One Character Erases a Word: Orthographic Noise, Tokenizers\\and Negation in Arabic Sentiment Classification}

\author{Anonymous submission}

\begin{document}
\maketitle

\begin{abstract}
Arabic tweets are full of orthographic variation that readers barely notice: the
elongation character tatweel, emphatic letter repetition, and inconsistent spelling of
hamza and final letters. We measure how this variation affects five Arabic and
multilingual encoders fine-tuned for three-way sentiment classification on two tweet
corpora, ArSarcasm-v2 and ArSAS, using about 40,000 controlled edits per model and three
training seeds. At the input level the effect is stark: in all four Arabic WordPiece
models, one tatweel turns the edited word into an unknown token, including every edited
negation word. Predictions are sturdier than this suggests. A tatweel in a single word
changes 3--7\% of predictions, and the same edit in 30\% of the words changes 9--18\%.
The extent to which a tokenizer destroys a word hardly predicts how often the prediction
changes (Spearman $\rho \le 0.18$). What differs is the cost: dense tatweel lowers
Macro-F1 by 3.5--6.2 points in the Arabic models but by only 1.4--1.5 points in XLM-R.
Writing tatweel on the negation word changes 2--3 points more predictions than writing it
on another word in the same tweet. Two annotators judged every sampled tatweel edit to
preserve meaning and sentiment, so these changes are errors. Removing tatweel and collapsing
letter runs before tokenization undoes these edits at no measurable cost on clean text. A
negation-aware normalizer we had proposed earlier adds nothing over the same rules
without its negation guard. We release the perturbation suite, leakage-safe splits,
predictions and the preregistered analysis plan.
\end{abstract}

\section{Introduction}

Social media Arabic is written with considerable freedom. Writers stretch a word with
the tatweel character for visual effect (\ar{جميـــل} for \ar{جميل} ``beautiful''),
repeat a letter for emphasis (\ar{حلووو}, \ar{كثيييير}), and often omit hamza or write
final \ar{ة} as \ar{ه}. In the two corpora we study, 3--5\% of tweets contain a tatweel
and a similar share repeat a letter three or more times (Table~\ref{tab:natural}).
Native readers glide over these variants. Whether sentiment classifiers do so is less
clear, because the tokenizers that feed them were built from vocabularies in which these
forms are rare or absent.

We arrived at this question through a negative result. A negation-aware normalization
method we developed earlier did no better than a simpler normalizer under any
condition. In that experiment, single-word edits applied to one MARBERT model produced
accuracy changes too small to separate from zero. We concluded that the design, not the
models, made the experiment uninformative. A single model gives no basis for
comparison. A single edited word per tweet is a weak treatment. The repetition edits
also skipped the long vowels \ar{ا}, \ar{و} and \ar{ي}, which carry most emphatic
repetition in real tweets.

This paper replaces that experiment with a broader, preregistered audit. We fine-tune
five encoders with three seeds each on two tweet datasets. We then apply four families
of orthographic edits at two densities, and in some conditions we edit the negation word
itself. Two annotators judged whether the edits preserve meaning and sentiment. We ask
four questions:
(RQ1) how often do realistic edits change predictions;
(RQ2) do tokenizer effects explain differences between models;
(RQ3) is editing the negation word worse than editing another word; and
(RQ4) does simple normalization before tokenization undo the damage?

The main findings are:
\begin{itemize}
\item Arabic WordPiece tokenizers map any word containing tatweel to \unk{}. This
includes negation words, so an edited tweet such as \ar{لـا} reaches the model with its
negation removed (\S\ref{sec:tokenizer}).
\item Predictions change far less than this input damage would suggest: tatweel in one
word changes 3--7\% of them, and tatweel in 30\% of the words changes 9--18\%. The \unk{} rate barely
predicts how many predictions change, but each WordPiece change costs about three times as
much Macro-F1 as a change made by XLM-R (\S\ref{sec:robustness}).
\item Tatweel on the negation word changes more predictions than tatweel elsewhere in
seven of eight model--dataset pairs. Elongating the negation word does not, but annotators
read that elongation as an intensity change rather than noise (\S\ref{sec:negation}).
\item Stripping tatweel and collapsing letter runs removes nearly all of these changes at
no measurable cost on clean text. The negation guard of our earlier method adds nothing
(\S\ref{sec:defenses}).
\end{itemize}

\section{Related work}

\paragraph{Noise and robustness.}
Both synthetic and natural character noise degrade neural models
\citep{belinkov2018synthetic}. Character-level recognizers have been proposed to defend
against misspellings \citep{pruthi-etal-2019-combating}, and behavioural test suites probe
whether a model is invariant to such edits \citep{ribeiro-etal-2020-beyond}. Our edits are
specific to Arabic script. We separate edits presumed to preserve meaning from a typo
control and verify that separation with human judgments. We also report the costs of a
defense alongside its benefits.

\paragraph{Arabic pretrained models.}
MARBERT \citep{abdul-mageed-etal-2021-arbert}, AraBERT \citep{antoun-etal-2020-arabert}
and CAMeLBERT \citep{inoue-etal-2021-interplay} use WordPiece vocabularies learned from
Arabic text. MARBERT and its successor share a vocabulary built from tweets. XLM-R
\citep{conneau-etal-2020-unsupervised} uses a multilingual SentencePiece vocabulary that
falls back on individual characters and therefore never produces an unknown token. The
recommended preprocessing for some Arabic models removes tatweel, but nothing in the
model interface enforces this. We are not aware of work that measures what omitting that
step costs a fine-tuned model.

\paragraph{Negation.}
Benchmarks under-represent negation, and models trained on them often ignore it
\citep{hossain-etal-2020-analysis}. We do not parse negation scope. Instead, we compare
an edit on the negation word with the same edit on another word in the same tweet.

\section{Study design}
\label{sec:design}

We preregistered the conditions, metrics, hypotheses and decision rules before observing
any model prediction on the new edits. The tokenizer audit in \S\ref{sec:tokenizer} was
run before the preregistration and is disclosed there.

\paragraph{Data.}
ArSarcasm-v2 \citep{abu-farha-etal-2021-overview} contains dialectal and MSA tweets
labelled negative, neutral or positive. We use a leakage-safe split that removes from
training any tweet whose normalized text occurs in the official test set (10,037 training
and 2,509 validation tweets). ArSAS \citep{elmadany2018arsas} contains 21,064 tweets with
an additional Mixed class, which we drop. We merge repeated tweet IDs and identical texts
into groups and exclude the 90 tweets whose groups carry conflicting labels, together
with 44 further copies linked to excluded tweets. A stratified
group split then gives 13,738 training, 1,966 validation and 3,923 test tweets. We
considered ASTD \citep{nabil-etal-2015-astd} as the second dataset and rejected it,
because 20\% of ArSarcasm-v2 training tweets (2,473) also occur in ASTD. ArSAS shares one
tweet with ArSarcasm-v2, and that tweet is excluded. Each model is trained and evaluated
separately on each dataset.

\centering\small
\begin{tabular}{lll}

Family & Original & Edited \\
\midrule
Tatweel & \ar{حلو} & \ar{حلـو} \\
Elongation $\times$2 & \ar{حلو} & \ar{حلووو} \\
Elongation $\times$4 & \ar{كثير} & \ar{كثيييير} \\
Folding & \ar{أحب}\,/\,\ar{جميلة} & \ar{احب}\,/\,\ar{جميله} \\
Typo (control) & \ar{جيد} & \ar{جبد} \\
Cue (tatweel) & \ar{لا} & \ar{لـا} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\caption{The edit families, illustrated on single words.}
\label{tab:examples}
\end{table}

\paragraph{Edits.}
Table~\ref{tab:examples} illustrates the four families.
\begin{itemize}
\item \emph{Tatweel} inserts one \ar{ـ} after the last letter that joins to the next.
\item \emph{Elongation} repeats the last internal long vowel, or the final letter if
there is none, two or four extra times.
\item \emph{Folding} writes \ar{أ}, \ar{إ} and \ar{آ} as \ar{ا}, final \ar{ة} as \ar{ه},
and final \ar{ى} as \ar{ي}.
\item \emph{Typo} replaces one interior letter with its neighbour on the Arabic keyboard.
\end{itemize}
The typo family was intended as a control that damages meaning. The human judgments in
\S\ref{sec:human} show that it does so only partly.

Each family is applied at two densities: \emph{single} edits one word, and \emph{dense}
edits $\lceil 0.3n \rceil$ of the $n$ Arabic words in the tweet. In \emph{cue} conditions
the edit falls on an unambiguous negation word (\ar{لا}, \ar{لم}, \ar{لن}, \ar{ليس},
\ar{مش}, \ar{مو}, \ar{مافي}, \ar{بدون} and their variants). We leave out \ar{ما}, whose
relative, interrogative and exclamative uses outnumber its negating use. Non-cue
conditions never edit a negation word. They also skip URLs, mentions, hashtags and
tokens attached to Latin characters. Which word gets edited is decided by hashing the
tweet ID and the condition. Single edits are a subset of the dense edits for the same
tweet, and both elongation levels edit the same character. Per condition, edits apply to
between 1,963 and 2,478 ArSarcasm-v2 tweets and between 1,657 and 1,951 ArSAS tweets.
Cue conditions apply to the 404 and 316 tweets that contain an editable negation word.

\paragraph{Models.}
We fine-tune MARBERT, MARBERTv2, AraBERTv02-twitter, CAMeLBERT-DA and XLM-R-base with one
fixed recipe:
\begin{itemize}
\item AdamW, learning rate $2{\times}10^{-5}$, batch size 16, at most five epochs;
\item early stopping and checkpoint selection on validation Macro-F1;
\item seeds 42, 43 and 44.
\end{itemize}
This gives 30 models. Revisions of all pretrained weights are pinned.
Table~\ref{tab:clean} reports clean validation performance.

\begin{table}[t]
\centering\small
\input{generated/clean_performance.tex}
\caption{Clean validation Macro-F1 (\%), mean $\pm$ standard deviation over three seeds.}
\label{tab:clean}
\end{table}

\paragraph{Defenses.}
At inference time we compare four preprocessors, each applied identically to clean and
edited text:
\begin{itemize}
\item \textsc{raw} leaves the input unchanged;
\item \textsc{std} removes tatweel and collapses runs of three or more identical letters
to a single letter;
\item \textsc{no\_ctx} and \textsc{nasn2} are the two conservative normalizers from our
earlier work.
\end{itemize}
\textsc{no\_ctx} and \textsc{nasn2} share all of their rules except one: \textsc{nasn2}
also declines to collapse repeated letters near a negation word. Their repetition rule
covers consonants only, so they do not undo elongated long vowels.

\paragraph{Metrics and statistics.}
The primary metric is the \emph{flip rate}, the share of edited tweets whose predicted
class differs from the prediction for the clean tweet. It needs no gold label and
isolates the effect of the edit. We also report Macro-F1 on clean and edited versions of
the same tweets and the difference between the two.

Intervals are 95\% percentiles of 2,000 cluster-bootstrap resamples. Clusters are groups
of duplicate texts, and the rate for each resample is averaged over the three seeds.
Contrasts are paired on identical tweets. These include cue versus non-cue, dense versus
single, a defense versus \textsc{raw}, and each WordPiece model versus XLM-R. A
hypothesis counts as supported for a model when its interval excludes zero in the stated
direction.

\paragraph{Deviations from the preregistration.}
We report two deviations. First, the preregistered zero-shot LLM was not evaluated
because the required GPU was unavailable. Second, this version reports the validation
partitions only. The preregistered single evaluation on the held-out test partitions
will be added once human adjudication is complete.

\section{What the tokenizer sees}
\label{sec:tokenizer}

\begin{figure*}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{figures/tokenizer_edits.pdf}
\caption{Number of tokens produced for an edited word, relative to the original word,
averaged over single-word edits. A hollow marker means the edited word becomes \unk{}
(rate 1.00 in every such cell). MARBERT and MARBERTv2 share a vocabulary, so their rows
coincide.}
\label{fig:tokenizer}
\end{figure*}

Figure~\ref{fig:tokenizer} shows, for every model and edit family, how many tokens an
edited word receives relative to the original. The pattern is identical on both datasets.

None of the four Arabic WordPiece vocabularies contains the tatweel character. WordPiece
therefore replaces any word containing it with a single \unk{}. This happens in 100\% of
tatweel edits, including all 404 (ArSarcasm-v2) and 316 (ArSAS) edited negation words. A
tweet containing \ar{لـا} thus reaches these models with no negation. XLM-R never
produces an unknown token. It instead splits a word containing tatweel into 2.5--2.6
times as many pieces, and an edited negation word into 2.9 times as many. Elongation
fragments the word in every model: four extra letters multiply its token count by
2.5--4.1. Folding is largely absorbed by MARBERT, whose lowercasing strips hamza from
alef. As a result, 35.5\% and 30.9\% of its single-word folding edits leave the token
sequence unchanged. The other models see nearly every folding edit.

\section{Do humans notice the edits?}
\label{sec:human}

\begin{table}[t]
\centering\small
\setlength{\tabcolsep}{4pt}
\input{generated/human_agreement.tex}
\caption{Agreement between the two annotators on 310 items (20 pilot items excluded).}
\label{tab:agreement}
\end{table}

\begin{table*}[t]
\centering\small
\input{generated/human_preservation.tex}
\caption{Items, out of 30 per condition, judged meaning-preserving by annotator A and by
annotator B, and items for which both annotators judged meaning preserved, or both
meaning and sentiment preserved.}
\label{tab:preservation}
\end{table*}

The study rests on the claim that most of these edits preserve meaning. To test it, two
native-speaker annotators independently judged 330 edited tweets drawn from the
ArSarcasm-v2 validation set, 30 per condition and one edit per tweet. They answered five
questions per item. Their first 20 items served as a pilot and are excluded from the
agreement figures. Agreement (Table~\ref{tab:agreement}) is high on every field. Cohen's
$\kappa$ is low for meaning preservation because almost every answer is ``yes''. Gwet's
AC1 \citep{gwet2008computing} corrects for this skew and gives 0.88. The 87 items on which
the annotators disagreed about preservation were sent to a third annotator. The counts
below use the stricter criterion that both annotators agreed.

The results (Table~\ref{tab:preservation}) separate the families clearly.
\begin{itemize}
\item \emph{Tatweel} preserved both meaning and sentiment in all 90 items, including the
30 in which it fell on a negation word. Any prediction change under tatweel is therefore
an error.
\item \emph{Elongation} preserved meaning in all 120 items, but it often changed
sentiment. Both annotators judged the sentiment unchanged in only 17 and 14 of 30 items
for one-word elongation by two and four letters, in 6 of 30 when 30\% of the words were
elongated, and in none of the 30 items with an elongated negation word. Readers take
repetition as emphasis, so a prediction change under elongation is not necessarily an
error.
\item \emph{Folding} preserved meaning in about 80\% of items.
\item \emph{Typos}, meant as the control, were often read through: both annotators judged
meaning preserved in 18 of 30 single-word items, though only in 8 of 30 dense items.
\end{itemize}

\section{How often do predictions change?}
\label{sec:robustness}

\begin{figure*}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{generated/flip_rates.pdf}
\caption{Flip rates with 95\% cluster-bootstrap intervals (\textsc{raw} inputs, three
seeds averaged per model). The full tables are in Appendix~\ref{app:tables}.}
\label{fig:flips}
\end{figure*}

\begin{table*}[t]
\centering\small
\input{generated/macro_f1_drops.tex}
\caption{Macro-F1 drop in points (clean minus edited, same tweets) under dense edits,
with 95\% intervals.}
\label{tab:drops}
\end{table*}

Figure~\ref{fig:flips} shows the flip rates. A single edited word rarely matters.
\begin{itemize}
\item Tatweel in one word changes 5.0--6.6\% of predictions on ArSarcasm-v2 and 3.0--3.9\%
on ArSAS.
\item Two extra letters change 2.5--6.8\%.
\item Folding changes 0.9--3.6\%.
\end{itemize}

Density matters a great deal. When 30\% of the words carry tatweel, flip rates rise to
11.8--17.5\% on ArSarcasm-v2 and 8.6--10.9\% on ArSAS. Dense elongation reaches 18.6\%
for XLM-R. Every dense-versus-single contrast for the three presumed-preserving families
is positive, in all five models and on both datasets (30 of 30; H1). The increases range
from 1.1 to 3.0 points for folding and from 5.5 to 11.9 points for tatweel and elongation.

\paragraph{Tokenizer damage barely predicts flip rates.}
The tokenizer audit predicts a large gap between WordPiece models, which lose the edited
word entirely, and XLM-R, which keeps a fragmented version. The gap is real but small.
Under dense tatweel, every WordPiece model flips more often than XLM-R on ArSarcasm-v2, by
3.1--5.7 points. On ArSAS only two of the four do so, by 1.6 and 1.7 points (H2: 6 of 8
contrasts). On ArSarcasm-v2, XLM-R is in fact the most sensitive model to dense elongation and to
dense typos.

Across the 55 model--condition cells per dataset, the share of edited words that become
\unk{} correlates only weakly with flip rate (Spearman $\rho$ = 0.18 and 0.14), and
fragmentation does not correlate at all ($\rho \le 0.03$). One explanation is that
fine-tuning already exposes the models to \unk{} for tatweel words: 4.6\% of
ArSarcasm-v2 training and validation tweets contain a natural tatweel.

\paragraph{But WordPiece errors cost more.}
The flip rate does not say whether a changed prediction is wrong. Table~\ref{tab:drops}
does. Under dense tatweel, Macro-F1 falls by 4.3--6.2 points for the WordPiece models on
ArSarcasm-v2 and by 3.5--4.0 points on ArSAS. For XLM-R it falls by only 1.5 and 1.4
points. Per changed prediction, a WordPiece model loses about three times as much Macro-F1 as
XLM-R. On ArSarcasm-v2, for example, MARBERT loses 0.38 Macro-F1 points per point of flip
rate, against 0.13 for XLM-R. This is consistent with an erased sentiment word
removing the evidence for the label rather than merely adding noise. Dense typos cost the
most: 5.4--10.9 points across all models.

\section{Negation as a stress test}
\label{sec:negation}

Natural noise on a negation word is rare. In the training and validation tweets, at most
five per corpus contain an elongated or tatweel-marked negation word. We therefore treat
the cue conditions as a controlled probe of how models represent negation, not as an
estimate of real-world risk.

For each tweet with an editable negation word, we compare editing that word with editing
another word in the same tweet (H3). Tatweel on the negation word, which turns it into
\unk{}, changes more predictions in seven of the eight WordPiece model--dataset pairs. The
increase is 2.4--3.3 points on ArSarcasm-v2 and 2.0--3.1 points on ArSAS. The exception
is CAMeLBERT-DA on ArSarcasm-v2 (+0.3, interval spanning zero). The effect is consistent
but modest. Losing the negation word changes the predicted class of roughly one additional
tweet in thirty to forty, so these models evidently do not rest their decisions on the
negation word alone.

Elongating the negation word (\ar{لاااا}) increases flip rates significantly in only two
of ten model--dataset pairs. The annotators read this edit very differently from tatweel.
Annotator A judged the sentiment changed in 26 of 30 items, and annotator B in 16 (with 13
marked unsure). In no item did both annotators judge it unchanged (\S\ref{sec:human}). An elongated \ar{لاااا} is an emphatic
refusal, and a model that changes its prediction may be reading it correctly.

\section{Does normalization help?}
\label{sec:defenses}

\begin{table*}[t]
\centering\small
\setlength{\tabcolsep}{4pt}
\input{generated/defenses.tex}
\caption{Flip rates (\%) under dense edits for each preprocessing defense, applied to both
clean and edited text.}
\label{tab:defenses}
\end{table*}

Table~\ref{tab:defenses} compares the defenses. \textsc{std} removes tatweel and collapses
letter runs, and so reverses exactly the edits it targets. It brings flip rates under
tatweel to zero and under dense elongation to at most 0.2\% (H4: 70 of 70 tests). It
does not touch folding or typos.

The more relevant question is what \textsc{std} costs on unedited text, where natural
letter runs may carry emphasis. The cost is negligible. On the clean validation tweets used in the tatweel conditions
(2,478 and 1,951), Macro-F1 under \textsc{std} differs from \textsc{raw} by at most 0.15
points for every model and dataset.

The two conservative normalizers from our earlier work remove most tatweel effects. They
leave 0.5--1.0\% of flips, because they keep tatweel inside the words they treat as
negation markers, which is a broader set than our cue list. They do not
undo elongated long vowels, which their repetition rule excludes. The negation guard that
distinguishes \textsc{nasn2} from \textsc{no\_ctx} changes nothing that matters. Across
110 paired contrasts the two differ by at most 0.2 points. None favours \textsc{nasn2},
and five favour \textsc{no\_ctx} by fractions of a point. Under the preregistered rule,
the claim that negation-aware normalization improves robustness is not supported (H5).

\input{generated/natural_noise.tex}
\caption{Validation tweets that already contain noise: flip rate (\%) between the tweet as

Controlled edits show what can happen; natural noise shows what does
(Table~\ref{tab:natural}). For the validation tweets that already contain noise, we
compare the prediction for the tweet as written with the prediction after \textsc{std}
cleaning (Table~\ref{tab:natural-flips}). Cleaning a natural tatweel changes 0--5\% of
predictions. Collapsing natural letter runs changes 11--15\% on ArSarcasm-v2 and 2--8\% on
ArSAS. The Macro-F1 differences on these slices are not significant: they contain only
42--123 tweets, and natural repetition carries genuine emphasis that cleaning removes.
Natural noise thus moves a noticeable minority of predictions, but this sample is too
small to show whether cleaning makes them more accurate.

\section{Discussion}

The tokenizer view and the prediction view tell different stories. A WordPiece model
receives an \unk{} in place of every tatweel word, which sounds catastrophic. Yet the
prediction usually survives, because sentiment in a tweet rarely depends on a single
word. Where the two views agree is in the cost of the predictions that do change. When an
Arabic WordPiece model loses a word and changes its prediction, the change costs about
three times as much Macro-F1 as a change made by XLM-R, which merely fragments the word.

The families also call for different readings. Tatweel is pure typography. Annotators saw
no change in 90 of 90 items, so every prediction change under tatweel is an error, and a
trivial fix removes it. Elongation is not noise in the same sense: readers took it as a
change of intensity in most items, and a model that responds to it is not necessarily
wrong. Benchmarks that treat all orthographic variation as a meaning-preserving
perturbation conflate these cases.

The practical recommendation follows directly. Anyone deploying an Arabic WordPiece model
on social media text should remove tatweel before tokenization. The cost on clean text
was below 0.15 Macro-F1 points in every model we tested. Collapsing letter runs is equally
cheap, but should be a deliberate choice, since it also removes emphasis. Negation-aware
exceptions to these rules did not help in our experiments.

\section*{Limitations}

The edits are rule-based and applied one family at a time, whereas real noise co-occurs.
The negation lexicon is finite and leaves out \ar{ما}. Checkpoints were selected on the
validation partitions, which favours clean accuracy but not the flip rate. The human
validation covers one dataset and 30 items per condition. Both datasets consist of
tweets, and other genres may behave differently. The preregistered LLM comparison and the
test-partition evaluation are not yet reported.

\section*{Ethics statement}

We use public research datasets under their licenses and release only tweet IDs, hashes,
labels and aggregate results, never tweet text. Two expert annotators labelled the
human-validation sample.

\section{Reproducibility}

Code, configurations and text-free artefacts are released with the paper. The artefacts
include perturbation logs, split manifests, predictions keyed by text hash, bootstrap
results and the preregistration. Every table in this paper is generated from the
released analysis bundle by a script; no number was entered by hand. Training is
deterministic for a fixed seed, GPU type and software stack, and checkpoint hashes are
published so that regenerated weights can be verified.
